tracks.name: Base Case & Accumulation
tracks.blurb: The two halves every recursive function needs, and trusting the call to have already solved the smaller problem.

tracks.name: Recursion Meets Structure
tracks.blurb: Nested lists, branching calls, and returning more than one thing at once -- the shapes trees need next.

problems.title: Factorial, the Smallest Possible Recursion
problems.blurb: One base case, one recursive case, nothing else -- get this reflex automatic first.
problems.statement:
Write factorial(n) recursively: n! is n * (n - 1) * ... * 1, and 0! is 1 by definition. Assume n >= 0.

Do not use a loop. The point of this problem is entirely the shape: one line that stops the recursion, one line that trusts factorial(n - 1) to already be correct and builds this call's answer on top of it.
hints: The base case is the smallest input you can answer without recursing at all: n == 0. What is 0! by definition?

For everything else, assume factorial(n - 1) already returns the correct answer for n - 1 -- don't try to trace through what it does internally. Given that trusted number, how do you build n!  from it?
return n * factorial(n - 1). Nothing more is needed.

tests.name: the base case itself
tests.src: assert factorial(0) == 1

tests.name: small values
tests.src:
assert factorial(1) == 1
assert factorial(2) == 2
assert factorial(3) == 6

tests.name: checked against a direct loop

problems.title: Summing a List Without a Loop
problems.blurb: The base case is the empty list -- and the recursive call already solved everything after the first element.
problems.statement:
Write sum_list(values), the sum of a list of numbers, without using a loop or the built-in sum.

The recursive step splits the list into its first element and "everything else": values[0] and values[1:]. Trust that sum_list(values[1:]) already correctly adds up everything after the first element -- don't try to reason about what happens two or three calls deep. Given that trusted number, what do you add to it?
hints: The base case is the empty list -- there is nothing to add, so what should an empty list sum to?
The recursive case: values[0] + sum_list(values[1:]). The slice values[1:] is a brand-new, one-shorter list -- that's what makes the recursion make progress toward the base case.
If you're tempted to write a loop inside this function, stop -- the recursive call is doing the loop's job. Each call handles exactly one element, then delegates the rest.

tests.name: the empty list sums to zero
tests.src: assert sum_list([]) == 0

tests.name: small lists
tests.src:
assert sum_list([5]) == 5
assert sum_list([1, 2, 3, 4]) == 10
assert sum_list([-3, 3]) == 0

tests.name: negative numbers throughout
tests.src: assert sum_list([-1, -2, -3]) == -6

tests.name: random lists, checked against the built-in sum
tests.src:
import random
random.seed(3)
for _ in range(200):
    values = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 12))]
    assert sum_list(values) == sum(values), values

problems.title: The Biggest Number, One Element at a Time
problems.blurb: Compare the first element against what the rest of the list already decided -- not against a value you invent.
problems.statement:
Write max_of_list(values): the largest number in a non-empty list, recursively, without the built-in max.

This is the exact shape a later tree problem needs, so it's worth getting the instinct right here first: the recursive call max_of_list(values[1:]) already correctly tells you the largest value among everything after the first element. Your only job at this call is to compare values[0] against that trusted number.

A list of one element has nothing to compare against and nothing left to recurse into -- that's your base case. Watch for negative numbers: a starting guess of 0 is wrong if every value in the list is negative.
hints: Base case: a list with exactly one element. Its max is that element -- there's nothing to recurse into.

Recursive case: rest_max = max_of_list(values[1:]). That call has already found the biggest value in everything after the first element. Now compare values[0] against rest_max directly -- don't seed a running variable from 0 or from values[0] alone and then loop.
return values[0] if values[0] > rest_max else rest_max.

tests.name: a single element is its own max
tests.src: assert max_of_list([7]) == 7

tests.name: small lists, max in different positions
tests.src:
assert max_of_list([3, 9, 2]) == 9
assert max_of_list([9, 3, 2]) == 9
assert max_of_list([3, 2, 9]) == 9

tests.name: all negative -- zero is not a safe starting guess
tests.src:
assert max_of_list([-5, -1, -9]) == -1
assert max_of_list([-1, -2, -3]) == -1

tests.name: random lists, checked against the built-in max
tests.src:
import random
random.seed(4)
for _ in range(200):
    values = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    assert max_of_list(values) == max(values), values

problems.title: Counting a Value Through Nested Lists
problems.blurb: No fixed depth to loop over -- a list inside a list inside a list, however deep, needs recursion to reach the bottom.
problems.statement:
A list can hold plain numbers and other lists, nested arbitrarily deep: [1, [2, 3, [4]], 5]. Write count_value(nested, target): how many times target appears anywhere inside, at any depth.

There is no way to know the nesting depth ahead of time, so a fixed number of loops can't reach the bottom -- recursion is the only way to handle "arbitrarily deep." This is exactly the shape of a tree's children list, just without a Node class wrapped around it.
hints: Loop over the elements of nested. For each one, check: is this element itself a list, or a plain number?
isinstance(item, list) tells you which case you're in. If item is a list, recurse into it: count_value(item, target). If it isn't, just compare it to target directly.
Keep a running total and add each element's contribution -- either count_value(item, target) for a nested list, or 1 (if it equals target) / 0 (if it doesn't) for a plain number.

tests.name: a flat list
tests.src: assert count_value([1, 2, 3], 2) == 1

tests.name: the empty list
tests.src: assert count_value([], 9) == 0

tests.name: repeats scattered across depths
tests.src: assert count_value([1, [2, 3, [2]], 2], 2) == 3

tests.name: deep nesting, a single match at the bottom
random nested lists, checked against a direct flatten

problems.title: Flattening a Nested List, Lazily
problems.blurb: yield from a recursive call -- the exact tool a tree's leaf-walk needs next.
problems.statement:
Write flatten(nested) as a generator that yields every non-list element inside nested, at any depth, left to right.

This is deliberately the same shape as walking every leaf of a tree -- just on plain nested lists instead of Node objects. The trap is the same one too: calling flatten(item) on a line by itself creates a generator and throws it away without yielding anything. You need yield from to forward what an inner call produces.
hints: Use yield, never build and return a list. Loop over nested: for each item, check isinstance(item, list).
If item is a plain value, yield item directly. If item is a list, you need everything it eventually yields, at whatever depth -- that's yield from flatten(item).
Writing flatten(item) alone (no yield, no yield from) on its own line does nothing observable -- it builds a generator object and immediately discards it without running any of its code.

tests.name: calling it returns a generator
tests.src:
import inspect
result = flatten([1, 2])
assert inspect.isgenerator(result), (
    "flatten returned %s -- use yield, not return" % type(result).__name__)

tests.name: flat and nested lists, left to right
tests.src:
assert list(flatten([1, [2, 3], 4])) == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert list(flatten([1, [2, [3, [4]]]])) == [1, 2, 3, 4]
assert list(flatten([])) == []

tests.name: the first value arrives without walking the rest
tests.src:
class Poisoned(list):
    def __iter__(self):
        raise AssertionError(
            "the rest of the list was walked before the first value was "
            "requested -- yield as you go, using yield from on nested "
            "lists")

late = [2, 3]
tail = Poisoned([late])
gen = flatten([1] + tail)
assert next(gen) == 1

tests.name: random nested lists, checked against a direct flatten

problems.title: Where the Biggest Number Is, Not Just What It Is
problems.blurb: A recursive call that has to hand back two things at once, because one of them alone can't answer the question.
problems.statement:
Write index_of_max(values): the index of the largest value in a non-empty list. If several elements tie for largest, return the index of the first one.

This is the same problem as max_of_list, with one twist that changes everything about the recursion: you now need to report where the max is, not just what it is. A recursive call on values[1:] that only returns an index isn't enough on its own — you can't tell whether values[0] beats it without also knowing what value that index points to. And a call that only returns the value isn't enough either — you'd have the number but no position.

The fix is to have the recursive call return both the best value and its index together, as a pair, so every level of the recursion has everything it needs to make its own comparison. Only the outermost call needs to throw away the value and keep just the index — which is exactly why a small helper that returns the pair, called once from inside index_of_max, is the natural shape here.
hints: Write a helper, best(values), that returns (value, index) for the best element -- the index is relative to whatever list was passed to that call, not the original list.
Base case of the helper: one element left. Its pair is (values[0], 0).

Recursive case: rest_value, rest_index = best(values[1:]). If values[0] is at least as big as rest_value, this call's answer is (values[0], 0). Otherwise it's (rest_value, rest_index + 1) -- the +1 shifts the index because rest_index was counted from the start of the shorter, sliced list, one position to the right of where values[0] sits.

Use >=, not >, in that comparison. values[0] is always to the left of everything best(values[1:]) considered, so on an exact tie it must win -- using a strict > lets the rest of the list keep a later duplicate instead of yielding to the earlier one.
index_of_max itself is one line: call best(values) and return only the index half of the pair.

tests.name: a single element is at index 0
tests.src: assert index_of_max([7]) == 0

tests.name: the max in different positions
tests.src:
assert index_of_max([3, 9, 2]) == 1
assert index_of_max([9, 3, 2]) == 0
assert index_of_max([3, 2, 9]) == 2

tests.name: ties resolve to the first occurrence
tests.src:
got = index_of_max([1, 5, 5, 2])
assert got == 1, ("got %d -- a later tie replaced the earlier one, use a "
                  "strict > comparison" % got)
got = index_of_max([5, 1, 5])
assert got == 0, got

tests.name: all negative values
tests.src: assert index_of_max([-5, -1, -9]) == 1

tests.name: random lists, checked against a direct scan

problems.title: Two Recursive Calls, Combined
problems.blurb: Branching recursion: each call spawns two more, the same way a tree node's children each spawn their own subtrees.
problems.statement:
Write fibonacci(n): the nth Fibonacci number, where fibonacci(0) = 0, fibonacci(1) = 1, and every later term is the sum of the two before it. Assume n >= 0.

Every problem so far had one recursive call per branch. This one has two — fibonacci(n - 1) and fibonacci(n - 2) — combined into one answer, the same way a tree node with several children combines each child's separately computed result. Getting comfortable with "make more than one recursive call, then combine what comes back" is the last piece before moving on to trees, where a node can have any number of children, not just two.

This one also has two base cases, not one — both fibonacci(0) and fibonacci(1) are answered directly, without recursing.
hints: Two base cases: n == 0 returns 0, n == 1 returns 1. Handle both before anything recursive.
For n >= 2: fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2). Each of those calls is trusted to already be correct on its own -- you don't need to trace through either one by hand.

This is slow for large n because the same smaller value gets recomputed many times across the branches -- that's fine for this problem, and it's exactly the same cost tradeoff an unpruned game tree has.

tests.name: both base cases
tests.src:
assert fibonacci(0) == 0
assert fibonacci(1) == 1

tests.name: the first several terms
tests.src:
assert fibonacci(2) == 1
assert fibonacci(3) == 2
assert fibonacci(4) == 3
assert fibonacci(5) == 5
assert fibonacci(6) == 8

tests.name: checked against a direct iterative computation
